## Future Research

Our findings suggest that custom AI-TAs can provide value when offering clear advantages over general-purpose alternatives like ChatGPT, particularly for accessing privately available information and recent specialized knowledge.

Future development will pursue both MPE-specific enhancements and broader pedagogical refinements. Custom AI-TAs (AI Teaching Assistants) are positioned against established alternatives like ChatGPT, with implementers advised to focus development on scenarios where a custom tool offers clear advantages [2, 5].

**Advantages of Custom AI-TAs for MPE:**
*   **Privately Available Information:** Custom AI-TAs can provide value for queries involving privately available information, such as specific quiz schedules [1, 2, 3, 6].
*   **Recent Specialized Knowledge:** They can access recent specialized knowledge before it appears in commercial training datasets. For example, a custom AI-TA provided accurate information on recent changes to FFmpeg 23 command-line syntax, which was documented in MPE course materials and needed for assignments, while ChatGPT lacked this knowledge [1, 2, 3, 6].
*   **MPE-Specific Enhancements:** Future development includes adding multi-modal capabilities to process visual content, which would benefit MPE students working with visual media and diagrams [1, 3]. There are also plans for daily recommendations for instructors based on student query patterns, enabling real-time teaching adaptation [1, 3].

**Advantages of ChatGPT:**
*   ChatGPT demonstrates exceptional performance on publicly available knowledge [2, 5]. Some students spontaneously mentioned ChatGPT when discussing the custom AI-TA, drawing both positive and negative comparisons, with one student noting, "I think its answers are not as good as chatgpt" [2, 5, 9].

In summary, while ChatGPT excels at general, publicly available knowledge, custom AI-TAs for MPE provide unique value by accessing private information and specialized, recent knowledge relevant to the course [1, 2, 3, 5, 6].

Whereas traditional digitization workflows require extensive and time-consuming color grading after scanning, multispectral scanning enables the calculation of color values corresponding to the spectral transmission of the scanned film through a dedicated rendering pipeline.', "Introduction
Over the last two decades, developments in film scanners have been largely incremental, even as the business model and areas of application have changed fundamentally.
Most professional film scanners in use today were conceived for chromogenic negative stocks intended for the Digital Intermediate Workflow of the early 2000s. When film production shifted fully to digital, scanner manufacturers repurposed their systems for archival use, making only minor modifications to their mechanical and optical designs. As digital technologies advanced and cinema projection also transitioned to digital, the dissemination of archival films became fully digital as well. This created a prolific field: Millions of hours of archival film required digitization, supported by both national initiatives and private funding schemes.
Yet despite the demand, awareness of the specific requirements of historical color film stocks by which we mean all the film color processes invented and in use before the mid-1990s -has remained limited.
The vast majority of the hundreds of color processes developed throughout film history differ fundamentally from chromogenic negatives. Their dyes and pigments exhibit idiosyncratic spectral characteristics that current scanners cannot comprehensively capture. Some of these colors are located outside of current standard color spaces (DCI-P3, Rec. 709, Rec. 2020). As a result, scans often fail to provide a complete and uncompromised representation suitable as a starting point for post-processing.
A new approach is therefore essential-one that spans the full spectral range of historical films and pays special attention to the illumination of these films. In film projection, the material composition of a film and the optical light path of the projector, combined with a specific illuminant, together define a film's unique appearance on the cinema screen.
Multispectral scanning addresses this challenge by recording the spectral characteristics of historical color films using a condensed illumination beam and providing the foundation for rendering the resulting scans with different projection illuminants used throughout film history. The ultimate aim of digitization is to recreate, as closely as possible, the appearance of the film as experienced in theatrical projection.
Equally important, every digitization must adhere to the core principles of restoration ethics: documentation, transparency, and reversibility. 1 Subjective interventions should be minimized. Abstract . The vast range of historical film color processes necessitates advanced workflows for scanning and post-processing to obtain digital representations that faithfully render the multitude of dyes and pigments present in archival materials. Our previous research indicates that optical configurations in traditional scanners limited to three or four spectral bands often fail to record important color information. To comply with core principles of future-proof digitization workflows, scanner properties and post-processing should be transparent, measurable, and science-based.
A multispectral digitization workflow that uses a uniform distribution of spectral bands across the visible spectrum can significantly improve results and provides reliable documentation of heterogeneous archival color film stocks. It also enhances versatility for innovative renderings compatible with future projection technologies and visualization pipelines.
Reducing subjective interventions in film digitization remains a cornerstone of restoration ethics. Multispectral scanning directly leverages the information embedded in historical film stocks, enabling a robust, material-based technology that respects the unique properties of each film element.
An integrated multispectral digitization and post-processing chain supports physically accurate rendering of scans by including measurements from various types of cinema projection illuminants. The ultimate goal of this workflow is to represent the color appearance as it would have been perceived on the cinema screen.

Film is an inherently ephemeral medium.
Film elements undergo continuous transformation during their lifespan-degradation, decay, fading, shrinking, damages such as scratches, dirt, microorganisms. Negatives, positives, and intermediate elements can co-exist in multiple versions. Distribution positives printed from original camera negatives or intermediates contain the intended color characteristics, provided they are unfaded and printed on the designated stock at the time of their production. Original camera color negatives, on the other hand, provide the highest spatial resolution and dynamic range, but lack crucial information for reproducing a film's authentic aesthetics. Some of them are using black-and-white separations as a source material to which color is applied only in the production of exhibition prints in the lab, for instance Technicolor's dye-transfer process. Earlier applied colors were added to each individual black-and-white print manually through tinting, toning, hand or stencil coloring, producing prints with widely varying palettes.

A rigorously science-backed multispectral scanning workflow ensures accurate color reproduction and authenticity for historical film by addressing the limitations of traditional methods and adhering to restoration ethics. While the provided documents primarily focus on historical film, the underlying principles of color science extend to advancements in automated color grading by providing objective, measurable, and consistent color management.

**Accurate Color Reproduction and Authenticity for Historical Film:**
1.  **Overcoming Traditional Scanner Limitations:** Most traditional film scanners use only three or four narrow spectral bands, which leaves gaps in sensitivity and fails to capture the full variability of spectral responses in historical film stocks. Their hardwired bands restrict versatility, and undocumented illuminants or proprietary image processing create "black-box" operations that violate restoration ethics [2]. In contrast, multispectral scanning employs a uniform distribution of spectral bands across the visible spectrum, recording the spectral characteristics of historical color films using a condensed illumination beam [7, 8]. This approach comprehensively captures the idiosyncratic spectral characteristics of historical film dyes and pigments that current scanners often miss [7].
2.  **Scientific Color Calculation:** Instead of subjective color grading, multispectral scanning enables the calculation of color values directly from the scanned film's spectral transmission [1, 6]. After multispectral scanning frame-by-frame with narrow-band illuminations, color values are computed from transmittance images using colorimetric calculations. These calculations account for a specific illuminant and the color-matching functions for a 2° CIE 1931 standard observer [3]. This process eliminates the need for costly, expert-dependent, and subjective color grading, thereby upholding the restoration ethic of transparency [1].
3.  **Recreating Theatrical Appearance:** The ultimate aim of this digitization workflow is to recreate, as closely as possible, the appearance of the film as experienced in theatrical projection [7, 8]. This involves considering the material and technical properties of historical film stocks, the spectral power distribution of scanner illuminants, and the light sources and optical paths of analog cinema projectors [5]. The workflow supports physically accurate rendering by incorporating measurements from various types of cinema projection illuminants [8].
4.  **Ethical and Future-Proof Approach:** This science-backed workflow minimizes subjective interventions, adhering to core restoration ethics of documentation, transparency, and reversibility [1, 7, 8]. It provides future-proof digital elements capable of adapting to emerging standards in color management and new display technologies [7]. It also offers a robust methodology to harmonize disparate film elements (e.g., negatives, positives, different film stocks) to achieve a consistent aesthetic representation with historical authenticity and high technical quality [4, 8].

**Extension to Advancements in Automated Color Grading for Modern Productions:**
While the documents primarily focus on historical film restoration, the principles and tools developed within this science-backed workflow lay a foundation for advancements in automated color grading:
1.  **Objective Color Data and Transformations:** The emphasis on precise, measurable color data derived from spectral characteristics, rather than subjective visual inspection, provides an objective basis for color management [1, 3, 8]. This scientific rigor allows for the creation of consistent and repeatable color transformations.

The digitization of existing content libraries, particularly non-digital physical media, is crucial for their long-term preservation and reuse. A significant challenge in this process, especially for historical film, is achieving accurate color reproduction and authenticity, which sometimes necessitates color correction after digitization to match the film's original release appearance.

To address this, a rigorously science-backed multispectral scanning workflow is utilized. This advanced method is essential because traditional scanners, with their limited spectral bands, often fail to capture the unique spectral characteristics of historical film colors, some of which fall outside current standard color spaces. Multispectral scanning, by employing a uniform distribution of spectral bands across the visible spectrum, directly extracts the inherent color information from historical film stocks. This material-based technology facilitates physically accurate rendering, with the ultimate goal of representing the color appearance as it would have been perceived on the cinema screen, thereby minimizing subjective interventions and upholding restoration ethics. The workflow integrates measurements of various historical cinema projection illuminants and employs colorimetric calculations with standard observers to compute color values directly from multispectral scans, eliminating the need for extensive, subjective color grading. This scientific methodology ensures transparency, sustainability, and reversibility, making the resulting digital elements future-proof and compatible with emerging display technologies.

This profound emphasis on color science also extends to advancements in modern color grading workflows, where it is being applied to automate the typically time-consuming and labor-intensive task of shot matching. Algorithms developed using color science and a colorist's approach focus on key aspects such as overall mood (color balance and exposure), faces, and objects, often incorporating machine learning techniques. Studies indicate that this automated approach can achieve approximately 70% of a colorist's grade while saving about 20% of the time, leading to a superior starting point and overall improved quality in less time. The output is intuitive and editable, offering control over balance, exposure, and flare.

['Technical implications
VC-6 with swXtch.io decouples the scale of AI inference from the constraints of source encoding and transport. The same core infrastructure can support new models, higher frame rates, or increased audience personalization without re-engineering the entire video path.', '3. Integration with swXtch.io AI Native Networking
SwXtch.io AI-native networking incorporates VC-6 in the network layer, so that video is prepared for AI consumption as it moves. The process starts at the swXtch AI Gateway, which ingests an ST 2110 feed and encodes it into VC-6 while also making the native ST 2110 signal available for traditional production workflows.
The encoded stream is delivered using the VC-6 MC protocol, an RTP over multicast transport that lets each AI consumer subscribe only to the level of quality or the regions it needs. This multicast distribution means that one VC-6 stream can serve many AI models in parallel, each receiving different subsets of the data without creating redundant encodes.', '- SMPTE ST 2110 : A set of standards for professional media over IP networks used for live production.
- SMPTE ST 2117 1 (VC-6) : The SMPTE standard that defines the VC-6 codec, a hierarchical intra frame format optimized for scalable decoding and AI processing.
- Tokenization : The process of converting decoded image data into numerical embeddings for AI models.', '8. Conclusion
VC-6 and swXtch.io form a codec and network combination that is built for the way AI consumes live video. By integrating hierarchical, region-aware encoding in a multicast fabric, the system moves much of the preprocessing workload out of standalone servers and into the transport layer.
This shift reduces redundant compute, lowers bandwidth, and allows multiple AI workloads to operate in parallel from a single encoded source. Models can dynamically request the resolution or image regions they need, which makes the workflow adaptive and resource-aware.
The result is a path to scalable and efficient AI native live video processing that works within industry standards and can be deployed in cloud or hybrid environments. For teams that want to
expand AI in live production without driving up cost or complexity, VC-6 with swXtch.io provides a practical foundation.', "Abstract
Artificial intelligence is becoming central to live media workflows, powering real-time object tracking, automated replay generation, camera switching, and personalized viewing experiences. These applications demand extremely low latency and efficient use of compute and network resources. Existing mezzanine formats such as JPEG 2000 and ProRes were designed for human viewing, not machine inference. They require full-frame decoding and multiple transcoding stages, which add delay, duplicate processing, and inflate infrastructure costs as AI workloads scale.
This paper introduces VC6, a hierarchical, region-aware codec standardized as SMPTE ST 2117-1, and demonstrates its integration with swXtch.io's AI-native multicast networking to enable selective, AI-ready live video transport. Unlike traditional codecs, VC6 supports multiresolution Levels of Quality (LOQ) and region-of-interest (ROI) decoding, allowing AI models to access only the portions of a frame needed for inference. AI-Native Live Video Workflows, particularly those utilizing VC-6 and swXtch.io, significantly enhance media production by directly addressing the limitations of traditional codecs and improving workflow efficiency for artificial intelligence (AI) applications [5].

**Addressing Traditional Codec Limitations:**
Traditional mezzanine formats like JPEG 2000 and ProRes were designed for human viewing, not machine inference. They require full-frame decoding and multiple transcoding stages, which introduce delay, duplicate processing, and inflate infrastructure costs as AI workloads scale [5]. VC-6, standardized as SMPTE ST 2117-1, is a hierarchical, region-aware codec specifically optimized for scalable decoding and AI processing [3, 5]. It is built for how AI consumes live video [4].

**Improving Workflow Efficiency:**
The integration of VC-6 with swXtch.io AI-native networking provides several key efficiencies:

*   **Decoupled AI Inference Scale:** This architecture decouples the scale of AI inference from the constraints of source encoding and transport, allowing for new models, higher frame rates, or increased audience personalization without re-engineering the entire video path [1].
*   **AI-Native Preprocessing:** SwXtch.io AI-native networking incorporates VC-6 into the network layer, preparing video for AI consumption as it moves. This shifts much of the preprocessing workload from standalone servers into the transport layer, reducing redundant compute and lowering bandwidth [2, 4, 7].
*   **Selective Data Access (ROI/LOQ):** Unlike traditional codecs that require full-frame decoding, VC-6 supports multi-resolution Levels of Quality (LOQ) and region-of-interest (ROI) decoding. This allows AI models to access only the specific portions of a frame and the quality level needed for inference, significantly reducing the amount of data processed. For example, object tracking can reduce per-frame decode data volume by up to 90% [5, 7, 10].
*   **Multicast Distribution for Parallel Workloads:** The VC-6 MC protocol uses RTP over multicast transport, enabling each AI consumer to subscribe only to the level of quality or regions it requires. A single VC-6 stream can serve many AI models in parallel, each receiving different subsets of the data without creating redundant encodes or proxy pipelines [2, 5, 6, 11]. This eliminates encoding duplication and network oversubscription, which often limit scale in multi-model live workflows [6].
*   **Parallel AI Processing:** The system supports a parallel model where multiple AI tasks (e.g., detection, tracking, segmentation, graphics generation) can run concurrently from the same source stream, each working at its required resolution and region. This minimizes redundant processing, improves throughput, and avoids the delays and bottlenecks of serial AI workflows [6, 8].
*   **Reduced Costs and Resources:** By eliminating redundant transcodes, separate transport paths, and allowing models to subscribe only to necessary data, the workflow reduces bandwidth, lowers cloud egress charges, and decreases intermediate storage needs for live clipping or partial replays [4, 11].

In summary, VC-6 with swXtch.io creates a practical foundation for scalable, energy-efficient, and standards-compliant AI-native live video workflows, offering a pathway for future interoperability within ST 2110 and related IP media ecosystems [4, 5].

ABSTRACT
Video consumption has grown rapidly worldwide, supported by advanced devices such as smartphones, tablets, and immersive headsets like Apple Vision Pro, which enable real-time 6 Degrees of Freedom (6DoF) navigation. Yet, the lack of engaging volumetric content limits applications in training and entertainment.
Volumetric video offers promise but faces challenges in natural 3D+t reconstruction, coding, and rendering due to high computational demands. In 2020, the ground-breaking Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) paper introduced a new way to generate natural free-viewpoint renderings of real scenes.
Follow-up research, including 3D Gaussian Splatting, improved efficiency and flexibility, though most approaches still require separate models per frame, complicating video representation. Recent extensions leverage temporal redundancy for compact, consistent, and editable volumetric video.
This paper reviews state-of-the-art radiance field–based methods, analysing their strengths and limitations, and provides an objective evaluation using a diverse multi-view dataset, with a focus on applications for entertainment and training.
**Keywords:**
volumetric video, neural radiance fields, 3D Gaussian Splatting, free-viewpoint rendering, immersive media
Introduction
Novel view synthesis (NVS) is a long-standing challenge of 3D computer vision: the rendering of unseen views of a scene from a set of captured views. NVS has a growing impact on a wide array of video applications including media consumption [1], sports retransmission [2], immersive training [3] and telepresence [4]. The applications fall into one of two categories: visual effects or immersive experiences. One common visual effect with NVS is the virtual rendering of non-captured camera movement. An illustrative example is the Intel True View technology [5], which proposes frozen time 360 degree replays of sports stadiums. In contrast, immersive experiences rely on real-time NVS to display position-dependent views to a user, allowing them to navigate freely within a virtual scene as if they were in the real location.
Early NVS methods interpolated viewpoints from depth information [6]. These methods were capable of rendering realistic novel views in ideal conditions, but they had limited light effect rendering capacity and were restricted to rendering views that were close to the reference views. Concurrently, novel devices, including the Apple Vision Pro, were making real-time 6 Degrees of Freedom (6DoF) tracking increasingly accessible. Free navigation of real scenes requires reconstructing a complete representation of the scene from recorded videos. In recent years, significant progress has been made towards volumetric-based approaches. One such approach is Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [7] which was first published in 2020. This method enables the generation of high-quality views by modelling the scene’s geometry and radiance. NeRF demonstrated the capacity of radiance field methods to represent complex real scenes with accurate light effects. Following the publication of NeRF, radiance fields have rapidly become the most regarded approach for NVS of natural content.
Early radiance field methods, including NeRF necessitated slow reconstructions for every scene to be performed, and could not render novel views in real time. New approaches have been derived from NeRF for faster processing [8], [9], higher quality rendering [10], [11] and more stable reconstructions [12]. The recent radiance field method 3D Gaussian Splatting techniques [13] have gained considerable popularity due to their demonstration of state-of-the-art rendering quality with in-real-time rendering capacity.
Building upon the latest advances in radiance field methods, the volumetric video field has undergone a rapid evolution in recent years. New techniques have extended the applicability of radiance field to a range of classical 2D video tasks, including semantic segmentation [14], streaming [15] and edition [16]. The development of real-time dynamic representations of radiance fields has opened the door to 6DoF+t navigable content in real-time.
However, each approach has its own advantages and drawbacks. We present an overview of NVS methods, focusing on radiance field approaches. We review the latest advances towards real-time 6DoF+t navigation and evaluate the state-of-the-art methods on a dataset of scenes showcasing complex human interactions in diverse environments.

The ongoing revisions to VSF TR-08 are actively integrating JPEG XS Temporal Differential Coding (TDC) into its JPEG XS transport framework over SMPTE ST 2110-22 [5, 8]. This integration is part of a broader effort by the Video Services Forum (VSF) to enhance clarity, consistency, and real-world interoperability in IP-based production environments [6, 9, 11]. TDC is a new predictive wavelet-based compression method that leverages previously compressed frames to improve coding efficiency while maintaining JPEG XS's ultra-low latency [6, 7].

To optimize deployment, particularly for bandwidth-constrained scenarios, specific capability sets are being defined:
*   **New Capability Sets for TDC** New capability sets for JPEG XS TDC are being added to TR-08 Section 10 (ST 2110-22) [5, 7]. These are designed to improve compression efficiency, especially for semi-static content, while preserving the ultra-low latency characteristics of JPEG XS [7].
*   **Low Bandwidth Use Cases** The revisions explicitly include "New Capability Sets for low bandwidth use cases" [6].
*   **Expanded Interoperability Points** The TR-08 revisions are also expanding interoperability points to include non-broadcast frame rates (e.g., 23.98, 24, 29.97, 30, and 60 fps) where TDC offers significant advantages. These expanded points are being added to TR-08 Capability Set A & AT (TDC) for 1080p FHD and 2160P UHD1, and TR-08 Capability Set B & BT (TDC) for 1080p FHD and 2160P UHD1 [10]. These additions provide more flexible and efficient compression options, which are crucial for optimizing deployment in various IP-based production environments, including those with bandwidth limitations.

The overall goal of these revisions is to ensure predictable network load and improve multi-vendor interoperability in live IP production and contribution [1].

The Video Services Forum (VSF) TR-08 outlines the transport of JPEG XS video within the SMPTE ST 2110-22 framework, designed for modern IP-based production environments to enable broadcast quality, virtually lossless compressed video transport with ultra-low latency. The ongoing revisions to TR-08 are actively incorporating Temporal Differential Coding (TDC) into this JPEG XS transport framework over SMPTE ST 2110-22. This integration includes defining new TDC capability sets, which will be added to TR-08 Section 10.

To optimize deployment in bandwidth-constrained scenarios, a specific capability set is being defined in the TR-08 revision for both JPEG XS with TDC and JPEG XS High Profile. This set aims to ensure that a stream will fit within a 1 Gbps link, including RTP/UDP/IP overhead, for TR-08 (ST 2110-22 over RTP). This capability set will include new interoperability points for non-broadcast frame rates and define a maximum Bpp of 2.0, with a Sublev 2bpp setting for resolutions such as 720p, 1080i FHD, 1080p, and 2160P UHD1. The efficiency of TDC allows for maintaining visually lossless quality at lower bitrates, which is crucial for these constrained links, ensuring cross-ecosystem compatibility without custom tuning.
